title: 2 Chronicles 14:9–15
context: Zerah the Ethiopian (Cushite) advances with a very large army and chariots to Mareshah. Asa meets him in the valley of Zephathah and prays, confessing that no one but the LORD can help the weak against the mighty, and that Judah relies on him. The LORD strikes the Ethiopians, who flee; Judah pursues them to Gerar, strikes the surrounding cities under the fear of the LORD, and returns with much plunder and livestock. This war is not recorded in Kings. Zerah’s identity is debated, and the numbers are given as the text states them.

verses.text: Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them with an army of a million troops and three hundred chariots, and he came to Mareshah.
verses.arminianNotes: Zerah the Ethiopian comes with a million troops and three hundred chariots to Mareshah. Arminian readers note that Zerah’s identity is debated; Cush often refers to the region south of Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the overwhelming force as setting up a test of trust. Both traditions state the numbers as given, and note that Mareshah lies in the lowland of Judah (Joshua 15:44), though its exact site is discussed.

verses.text: Then Asa went out to meet him, and they set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa goes out and sets the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah. Arminian readers note that Asa acts courageously, meeting the enemy rather than hiding behind his fortifications.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Asa preparing for battle while preparing to pray. Shared ground: the location of Zephathah is uncertain, and both traditions read the verse as setting the scene for Asa’s prayer.

verses.text: Asa cried to the LORD his God, and said, “LORD, there is no one besides you to help, between the mighty and him who has no strength. Help us, LORD our God; for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. LORD, you are our God. Don’t let man prevail against you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Asa prays that there is no one but the LORD to help the weak against the mighty, and that Judah relies on him. Arminian readers see a model of trusting prayer, offered in a moment of overwhelming danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Asa’s prayer as appealing to God’s honor: “Don’t let man prevail against you.” Shared ground: both traditions agree that God honors trust and judges self-reliance, and neither forces a fork here.

verses.text: So the LORD struck the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled.
verses.arminianNotes: The enemy breaks and runs as the LORD strikes them before Judah. Arminian readers see Asa’s plea in the previous verse answered at once, with no account of tactics at all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s power displayed on behalf of his people. Both traditions read the verse as the immediate answer to 14:11, showing that the outcome came from God rather than from Judah’s numbers.

verses.text: Asa and the people who were with him pursued them to Gerar. So many of the Ethiopians fell that they could not recover themselves, for they were destroyed before the LORD and before his army. Judah’s army carried away very much booty.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa pursues to Gerar, and the Ethiopians are destroyed before the LORD and his army. Arminian readers note the phrase “before the LORD,” which presents the battle as God’s own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Judah’s army as the LORD’s army in this battle. Shared ground: Gerar’s location is debated, though it lay in the southwest (compare Genesis 20:1), and both traditions read the verse as completing the victory.

verses.text: They struck all the cities around Gerar, for the fear of the LORD came on them. They plundered all the cities, for there was much plunder in them.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah strikes the cities around Gerar, for the fear of the LORD came on them. Arminian readers note that the fear of the LORD falls on the surrounding peoples, as in earlier stories of Israel’s history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working on the hearts of Judah’s enemies. Both traditions read the verse as part of the victory narrative, reported as the text gives it without endorsement of every detail of the plunder.

verses.text: They also struck the tents of those who had livestock, and carried away sheep and camels in abundance, then returned to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah strikes the tents of herdsmen and carries off sheep and camels before returning to Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the campaign ends with a return to the capital, and with plunder that will later be offered (15:11).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the abundance as part of God’s provision for his people after the victory. Shared ground: the verse closes the war account, and both traditions read it as narrative rather than as a model for conduct.
